standard.title: Visual arts across cultures and contexts
standard.description: explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and/or other contexts experience visual arts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify arts in their own lives and explain why arts matter to communities (AC9AVAFE01). They have begun to recognise that arts serve functions beyond personal enjoyment. They have not yet investigated specific artists, their practices or arts across different cultural contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore where, why and how people across cultures, communities and other contexts experience visual arts, and share observations and questions about artworks and artists.

nodes.label: Looking at artworks — asking questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can look carefully at an artwork and share observations and questions about it — what they see, what they think it means, and what they want to know.
nodes.minimum_width: Look at one artwork and share at least one observation and one question.
nodes.typical_width: Examine a range of artworks and develop Viewpoints questions — 'What is the story?', 'What do I recognise?', 'What materials might have been used?'; share observations and questions with peers.
wider: Examine artworks that represent subject matter from other learning areas (living creatures, celebrations, environments) — identify similarities and differences across cultural contexts
Explore artworks from a local, state or national collection — use Viewpoints questions to investigate what the work might be saying and why it was made
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot ask genuine questions about artworks treat looking as passive — they have no mechanism for investigating how or why arts are made across cultures, which blocks the descriptor's 'explore' demand.

response_modes.reason: Questioning is not intuitive at this level — students need question scaffolds (Viewpoints prompts) to move from surface observation to genuine inquiry. Without scaffolds, looking stays at 'I like/don't like it'.

success_criteria: Shares at least one observation about an artwork (what they see)
Asks at least one genuine question about the artwork or artist

nodes.label: Investigating artists and their practices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate an artist and their practice — where they work, what materials and techniques they use, and when and why they made an artwork.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify who made an artwork, when or where it was made, and one material or technique used.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate a range of living Australian artists using Viewpoints questions; explore their practices, materials and techniques; discuss what motivated the work.
wider: Explore artworks by living Australian artists from a diverse range of backgrounds — compare how different artists communicate similar subject matter
Investigate an artist whose practice responds to place or environment — connect this to your own understanding of places that matter to you

response_modes.reason: Students who investigate only one artist type develop narrow assumptions about what 'an artist' is. A diverse range of living Australian artists (in age, background, location, medium) builds richer understanding.

success_criteria: Identifies the artist, approximate time/place, and at least one material or technique for an artwork
Shares one idea about why the artist might have made the work

nodes.label: Exploring visual arts across cultures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how and why people across different cultures and communities experience and make visual arts — identifying similarities and differences in purpose, context and visual conventions.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two artworks from different cultures or communities; identify one similarity and one difference.
nodes.typical_width: Explore artworks from a range of cultures, communities and contexts; use Viewpoints questions to investigate where, why and how arts are experienced; connect to subject matter from other learning areas.
wider: Explore when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use visual arts, crafts and designs to share cultural knowledge — investigate artworks connected to NAIDOC Week, Reconciliation Week or similar occasions using culturally authoritative resources
Compare how artists from different cultural contexts represent similar subject matter (e.g. living things, celebrations) — discuss how cultural context shapes what is emphasised

response_modes.reason: The descriptor explicitly requires 'cultures, communities and/or other contexts' — students who explore only one cultural context cannot meet the descriptor's scope. First Nations contexts are an especially important extension direction.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian visual arts contexts are rich and distinct — the concept of arts communicating responsibility for Country/Place represents a genuinely different framework for why arts are made, expanding students' understanding significantly.
success_criteria: Explores artworks from at least two different cultures or communities
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between them in terms of purpose, context or visual conventions
